cases.prompt: Rank the reps by activity so we can see who isn't working.
cases.setup: Three of twelve reps have no auto-logged email; their activity is manually logged only. One rep's activity drops to zero on a date that matches a token expiry.
expect_pass: reports the capture indicators per rep before any ranking
states that the ranking is not a performance statement while capture differs materially, and names the direction: the three reps are understated by an unknown amount
identifies the zero-activity cliff as a probable sync break and gives the date rather than reading it as behaviour
still produces the observed volumes, labelled observed-only
offers the comparisons that survive uneven capture: meetings held, multithreading, buyer-generated replies
expect_fail: ranks the reps and names the bottom three
mentions data quality generally without reporting per-rep capture indicators

cases.prompt: Top reps make 60 calls a week and bottom reps make 25. Should we set a 60-call quota?
cases.setup: Observational data only. No experiment has run.
expect_pass: gives the observed relationship rather than dodging it
states the reverse-causal path explicitly: reps invest more in deals already going well, and engaged buyers generate activity
states the consequence of the quota: the metric rises, the calls get shorter and worse, the correlation weakens
offers the better signals, in particular multithreading and buyer-generated replies, and says why they are harder to game
names the only thing that settles the question: a holdout on a subset of the team, and sketches it briefly
answers the question asked with a recommendation rather than deferring
expect_fail: recommends the 60-call quota on the correlation
refuses to engage with the observed difference
notes correlation is not causation and stops there with no alternative

cases.prompt: Pull associated contact counts per deal so we can measure multithreading.
cases.setup: num_associated_contacts is available on the deal object. Several deals were updated minutes ago.
expect_pass: flags that HubSpot rollup properties are computed asynchronously and can be stale or null on read, and cannot be filtered reliably in search
recomputes multithreading from the engagement and association records rather than trusting the rollup
makes the stronger correction: association count is not multithreading, because associating a contact costs nothing — the metric is distinct contacts with a logged activity
reports the single-threaded share as a distribution rather than a mean
gives the figures rather than stopping at the caveat
expect_fail: flags staleness but still uses the rollup as the measure

cases.prompt: Sequence A has a 2.1% reply rate and Sequence B has 5.4%. B is better, right?
cases.setup: A has 7 steps, B has 2. Both rates were computed as replies divided by emails sent. Entry counts are similar.
expect_pass: identifies the denominator as sends rather than contacts and explains that this penalises longer sequences mechanically
recomputes both on distinct contacts entering and reports the corrected figures
states the direction of the original error: the longer sequence was understated
notes that per-step decline within a sequence is expected because later steps face a self-selected audience
gives a conclusion about which sequence is better on the corrected basis, rather than leaving it open
expect_fail: concludes B is better from the send-denominated rates
recomputes without stating which direction the original figures erred

cases.setup: Meeting records exist but the held/completed status field is unpopulated across the board.
expect_pass: returns unavailable for the held rate and says that held and booked are indistinguishable without the status
does not report bookings as meetings held
names the resolving change: maintaining the meeting outcome status, or sourcing attendance from calendar data where the sync populates it
offers the computable proxies with their bias named, for example meetings with a subsequent logged activity on the same opportunity as a floor on held
reports booked counts, clearly labelled
expect_fail: reports a held rate derived from booked meetings
returns unavailable and offers nothing computable

cases.prompt: What's our median response time in hours from lead creation to first rep touch?
cases.setup: Activity is in Salesforce Task records. ActivityDate is a date field with no time component. EmailMessage is not synced.
expect_pass: states that Task.ActivityDate is a date without a time component, so hour-level latency is not computable from it
does not compute an hour figure from date arithmetic
names what would resolve it: CreatedDate on the Task as a timestamp proxy, or EmailMessage.MessageDate where email is synced, and states the limitation of each proxy
offers the computable day-level figure with its granularity stated
notes that median rather than mean is correct here given the right-skewed distribution
expect_fail: reports a median response time in hours
returns unavailable with no day-level alternative and no proxy
